summary: Describes a mechanism for signaling active or standby status of redundant pseudowires between their end points, so provider edge nodes agree on which one carries traffic. It applies to single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires.

eli5.summary: Two roads lead to the same place. This is how both ends agree which is the main road for today and which is the spare.

questions: what is the pseudowire preferential forwarding status bit
how does pw redundancy choose the active pseudowire
what is independent mode vs master slave mode pseudowire
subtitle: A status bit that lets two ends of a redundant pseudowire set agree which one is active and which are on standby.

tldr.problem: When several redundant pseudowires connect the same two provider edge nodes, both ends must pick the same one to carry user traffic, or packets are lost.
tldr.mechanism: A new Preferential Forwarding bit in the PW Status TLV signals active or standby for each pseudowire, and a second Request Switchover bit lets one end ask the other to move to a different pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: Two modes are defined, independent and master/slave. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4447 and is itself updated by RFC 7771.

today: RFC 6870 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4447 and is listed as updated by RFC 7771; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC text does not describe any deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6870 provides the control-plane extensions that support the protection schemes of pseudowire redundancy described in RFC 6718. A set of redundant pseudowires (PWs) is configured between Provider Edge (PE) nodes in single-segment applications, or between Terminating PE (T-PE) nodes in multi-segment applications. The RFC defines a new status bit so the PEs can tell each other which PW is the preferred one to use.

Without faults, every PW can be up, and a PE must still pick a single active PW for user packets. All others are standby and must not carry user packets. The existing PW status codes from RFC 4447 only report faults, so a new bit is needed.

The RFC supports 1:1 and N:1 protection, a locally configured precedence (lowest value wins), and primary/secondary PWs with optional revertive switching. 1+1 protection, with traffic permanently duplicated on both paths, is not supported. Redundancy where the PW segments terminate on a Switching PE (S-PE) is left for further study.
sections.eli5: If you have a main road and spare roads, someone has to say which road is in use. This RFC adds a flag that says it.

sections.title: Independent Mode
sections.content:
In independent mode, each PW endpoint decides for itself which PWs it is willing to make active and advertises that choice. A PW is actually active only when it is up at both endpoints and both endpoints advertise active. If it is up but either end says standby, it is in standby: endpoints MUST NOT forward data over it, though they MAY allow OAM packets such as VCCV and specific control plane packets.

The status is carried in the PW Status TLV. A cleared Preferential Forwarding bit means active, and a set bit means standby. The state is sent in the initial label mapping message and in later notification messages when it changes.

If more than one PW qualifies as active, both PEs MUST use a common selection rule. The default, which all implementations MUST support, picks the PW with the lowest PWid for the PWid FEC. For the Generalized PWid FEC, it compares the AGI::SAII::TAII triplet, with the PE having the lowest system IP address using AGI::SAII::TAII and the highest using AGI::TAII::SAII so both compare the same value. A PW endpoint MAY instead use configured precedence or primary/secondary designations. If no active PW can be found, a management notification SHOULD be generated.
sections.eli5: Both ends say which road they like. They only use a road when both said yes, and when there is a tie they use the same simple rule, like picking the lowest number.

sections.title: Master/Slave Mode and Its State Machine
sections.content:
In master/slave mode one endpoint, the master, chooses the PW and the other endpoints, the slaves, MUST follow. The master sets the Preferential Forwarding bit to active on the chosen PW and to standby on the rest, and it MUST ignore the bit received from slaves. Roles are assigned by local configuration. The RFC does not define a way to detect misconfiguration or a backup master, and recommends independent mode where PE node protection is required.

If the master uses primary/secondary and precedence rules, it MUST pick the lowest precedence value, prefer the primary PW over secondaries, and revert to the primary immediately or after a configurable delay once it is available again. On the slave side, when the received bit goes from active to standby the slave MUST stop forwarding, and when it goes from standby to active the slave MUST start.

To reduce the number of LDP status messages, PWs may be grouped with a common Group ID or PW Grouping ID TLV so a single wildcard notification covers all of them. For multi-segment PWs, S-PEs MUST relay the status bits between segments.
sections.eli5: One friend is the leader and picks the road. The other friends just do what the leader's flag says.

sections.title: Coordinating a Switchover
sections.content:
Some applications need both ends to move to the same PW together. The RFC defines a second bit, Request Switchover, for this. Unlike master/slave mode, the requesting endpoint needs an explicit acknowledgment before it moves, and either endpoint may start a request. A PE MAY support the bit, and a PE that does not support it ignores it.

The requester sends a status TLV in an LDP notification with the bit set on the PW it wants. It does not start forwarding on that PW yet, though it MAY enable receiving. It starts a timer that SHOULD be configurable with a default of 3 seconds. If the peer answers by clearing its Preferential Forwarding bit on the requested PW, that is the acknowledgment: the requester stops the timer, activates the PW, clears its bits on the new PW and sets the Preferential Forwarding bit on the old one.

The receiver, on getting a request for a different PW that is up, activates it and sends the same pair of updates. A request for a PW that is down MUST be ignored. If both ends request at once, the one with the higher address ignores the peer's request and keeps waiting, while the one with the lower system IP address aborts its timer and acts as the receiver. If the timer expires, the request is assumed rejected and a new one MAY be sent.
sections.eli5: One side asks, can we switch to the other road? It waits a few seconds for a yes. Once the other side says yes, both switch together.

sections.title: Applicability and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
These mechanisms are for applications that need standby signaling for a PW or group of PWs. Both the PWid FEC and the Generalized PWid FEC are supported, all PWs in a redundant set MUST use the same FEC type, and each PW must be uniquely identified. A PE using them MUST negotiate the PW Status TLV with its T-LDP peers per RFC 4447; if either end does not support it, the mechanisms cannot be used.

A PE that does not support the new bits MUST ignore them when a peer sets them. The RFC updates RFC 4447 in two ways: any status bit not originally defined in RFC 4447 must be ignored by an implementation that does not support it, and a status bit may now signal something other than a fault, including an instruction to the peer PE.

The RFC also says status mapping for AC and PW defects follows the rules of another document, with the change that a PE entering an AC defect state sends the defect indication over all PWs in the redundant set tied to that AC.
sections.eli5: If one side does not know the new flags, it just ignores them, so older equipment keeps working.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The new status bits have the same security considerations as the PW setup and maintenance protocol in RFC 4447, so LDP extensions and options that protect PWs must be implemented. The RFC adds that the security of a redundant PW set is only as good as the weakest security on any of its members.
sections.eli5: A chain is as strong as its weakest link, and a set of spare roads is only as safe as the least safe one.

sections.title: Status Codes Registered with IANA
sections.content:
Two codes were allocated from the Pseudowire Status Codes registry. 0x00000020 is the Preferential Forwarding bit: set means PW forwarding standby, cleared means PW forwarding active. 0x00000040 is the Request Switchover bit: set means a request to switch over to this PW, cleared means no specific action.

The RFC says new MIB objects for PW redundancy will be defined in a separate document.
sections.eli5: The two new flags were given their own spots on the official list of flags so nobody else uses them.
